subject: Copywriting
title: Research Before Writing
description: A quick, practical guide to Research Before Writing.

hook.text: Ogilvy spent three weeks reading about Rolls-Royce before writing one word. Hopkins tested everything before scaling.

buildup.text: Every legend researched obsessively. Schwartz studied markets for months.

discovery.text: The common thread: great copy comes from understanding, not inspiration. The writing is 20%; the research is 80%.

twist.text: Modern copywriters often skip research and rely on templates.

climax.text: The copywriting legends agree on one thing: know your audience, your product, and your market before writing a word.

punchline.text: Research 80%, write 20%. Every legend agrees on this.

quiz.question: How much of great copywriting is research according to the legends?

details.summary: Every great copywriter from Hopkins to Ogilvy to Schwartz insisted that research was the most important phase of the writing process. Ogilvy spent weeks researching before writing a single word. Schwartz read everything his audience read. The legends agree: great copy is assembled from research...
details.whyItMatters: Research eliminates guesswork and grounds copy in real customer language and real product truths. Writers who skip research produce generic work; those who embrace it produce copy that converts.
takeaways: Ogilvy spent weeks researching before writing a single headline
Research reveals the specific language customers use to describe problems
The best copy is assembled from facts, not invented from imagination

faq.question: How much research should a copywriter do before writing?
faq.answer: Legendary copywriters typically spent more time researching than writing. Ogilvy read everything about a product before starting. Eugene Schwartz spent a week reading before drafting. As a rule, gather at least three times more material than you think you need.

faq.question: What kind of research produces the best copy?
faq.answer: Customer research — reviews, interviews, support tickets, forums — is most valuable because it reveals real language and real pain points. Product research comes second. Competitor research helps identify gaps. The best copy draws from all three sources.
